JP-EX-01-001.notes: あく is intransitive (the door opens, with が); あける is transitive (I open the door, with を). Japanese has many such pairs, and the particle is the clue: が for 'it happens', を for 'someone does it'.

JP-EX-01-002.notes: 始まる (intransitive): 授業が始まる 'class starts'. 始める (transitive): 先生が授業を始める. English 'start' covers both, so learners often mix them up.

JP-EX-01-003.notes: つく (intransitive): 電気がつく 'the light comes on'. つける (transitive): 電気をつける 'switch on the light'. The pair also covers TVs and air conditioners.

JP-EX-01-004.notes: 落ちる (intransitive): コップが落ちる 'the glass falls'. 落とす (transitive): コップを落とす 'drop the glass'. 落とす also means 'lose' small things: さいふを落とした.

JP-EX-01-005.notes: こわれる (intransitive): パソコンがこわれる 'breaks (down)'. こわす (transitive): 弟がこわす 'my brother broke it'. The transitive version assigns blame.

JP-EX-01-006.notes: 起きる (intransitive): 子どもが起きる 'wakes up'. 起こす (transitive): 母が子どもを起こす 'wakes the child'. 起こす also means 'cause': 事故を起こす.

JP-EX-01-007.notes: 止まる (intransitive): 車が止まる 'the car stops'. 止める (transitive): 警察が車を止める 'the police stop the car'. 止める is also 'park': 車を止める.

JP-EX-01-008.notes: わく (intransitive): お湯がわく 'water boils'. わかす (transitive): お湯をわかす 'boil water'. お湯 is hot water; 水 is always cold or room temperature.
JP-EX-01-008.tip: お湯 = hot water; 水 = cold water.

JP-EX-01-009.notes: しまっている (intransitive + ている) states that the window is shut, with no one implied. しめてある (transitive + てある) means someone shut it on purpose and it stays shut.
JP-EX-01-009.tip: Intransitive + ている = a state; transitive + てある = left that way on purpose.

JP-EX-01-010.notes: 出る (intransitive): 家を出る 'leave home', where を marks the place left, not an object. 出す (transitive): ごみを出す 'put out the rubbish'. Japanese rubbish goes out on set days.

JP-EX-02-001.notes: ている on a change-of-state verb describes the resulting state: 結婚しています 'is married', not 'is getting married'. The wedding happened in the past; the state continues.
JP-EX-02-001.tip: 結婚している = is married (a state).

JP-EX-02-002.notes: 来ています 'has come and is here'. With 来る and 行く, ている means 'is there now', not 'is on the way'. For 'on the way', use 向かっています.

JP-EX-02-003.notes: 勤めています 'works at (is employed by)'. 勤める describes employment, so ている gives the ongoing job. 働く would focus on the activity of working.

JP-EX-02-004.notes: 知っています means 'know', but the negative is 知りません, not ×知っていません. 知る describes coming to know; the ている form is the state of knowing.
JP-EX-02-004.tip: Know = 知っている; don't know = 知らない.

JP-EX-02-005.notes: の turns a clause into a noun for things perceived directly: 遊んでいるのが見える. こと is for abstract facts, and is required in 趣味は…ことです.
JP-EX-02-005.tip: Perception verbs take の; 趣味は… takes こと.

JP-EX-02-006.notes: 走っているのを見ました 'saw him running'. 見る, 聞く and 見える take の for a scene you witness; こと would be wrong here.

JP-EX-02-007.notes: ことができる requires こと: 話すことができます. の can't replace it in this fixed pattern, nor in ことにする or ことがある. 話す is in the dictionary form.

JP-EX-02-008.notes: は after an object, replacing を, marks contrast: たばこはすいません 'cigarettes, I don't smoke'. The first clause sets up the contrast: お酒は飲みますが.
JP-EX-02-008.tip: Contrastive は replaces を and が.

JP-EX-02-009.notes: は after another particle adds contrast: 東京には行った 'to Tokyo, at least'. には, では, からは, とは are all common.

JP-EX-02-010.notes: が marks the subject inside a clause that describes a noun: 私が作ったケーキ. は can't be used inside such a clause, since it marks the topic of the whole sentence.
JP-EX-02-010.tip: Inside a relative clause, the subject takes が.

JP-EX-02-011.notes: が inside a とき clause: 母が帰ってきたとき. The main sentence has its own topic, 私は. Two subjects, two particles.

JP-EX-02-012.notes: あの refers to something both speakers know from shared memory; その refers to something just mentioned that the listener doesn't know. Using あの for a new shop would sound odd.
JP-EX-02-012.tip: Shared memory → あの; just mentioned → その.

JP-EX-02-013.notes: やる means 'give' to plants, animals or people below you: 花に水をやる 'water the flowers'. Many speakers now prefer あげる, even for plants.
JP-EX-02-013.tip: やる to people sounds rough; あげる is safer.

JP-EX-02-014.notes: 犬にえさをやる 'feed the dog'. えさ is animal food; for people, ごはん. あげる is increasingly common with pets. The past やりました reports a routine act.

JP-EX-02-015.notes: を with motion verbs marks the route: 道を渡る 'cross the road'. It isn't an object; the road isn't acted on. Likewise 公園を歩く, 橋を渡る.
JP-EX-02-015.tip: Motion verbs: を marks the route or the place left.

JP-EX-02-016.notes: を marks the vehicle you get off: 電車を降りる 'get off the train'. Getting on uses に: 電車に乗る. Learners often say ×電車から降りる, which is possible but less standard.

JP-EX-02-017.notes: を marks the place left with 出る: 大学を出る, literally 'leave university', which also means 'graduate'. ずっと + ている shows the job has lasted ever since.
JP-EX-02-017.text: 大学{{c1::を::particle: out of (leaving)}}出てから、ずっと東京で働いています。
JP-EX-02-017.tr: Since leaving university, I've worked in Tokyo.
JP-EX-02-017.flag: dup: replaced 毎朝、八時に家を出ます (same sentence as part of EX-01-010)

JP-EX-03-001.notes: てる is the casual contraction of ている: してる. In casual speech the い disappears in all forms: してた, してない.
JP-EX-03-001.tip: ている → てる; ていた → てた.

JP-EX-03-002.notes: 知ってる 'I know'. It's the default form among friends; 知っている would sound stiff. よ adds 'I'm telling you'.

JP-EX-03-003.notes: とく is the casual contraction of ておく: 買っておく → 買っとく. It means doing something in advance, here getting drinks before guests arrive.
JP-EX-03-003.tip: ておく → とく; でおく → どく.

JP-EX-03-004.notes: 置いとく 'I'll leave it here'. ておく here means leaving something in place for later. 置く = put, place. The prefix-like contraction keeps the meaning: leave it here for now, for later use.

JP-EX-03-005.notes: じゃう is the casual contraction of でしまう: 飲んでしまう → 飲んじゃう. 飲む gives で because its て-form is 飲んで. ジュース = juice, soft drink.
JP-EX-03-005.tip: Verbs with a で て-form (飲んで, 読んで) take じゃう.

JP-EX-03-006.notes: ちゃった is the casual past of てしまった: 行っちゃった 'has gone (and I missed it)'. The regret is built in. 電車 is the subject: the train has left.

JP-EX-03-007.notes: じゃ is the casual contraction of では: 泳いでは → 泳いじゃ. It's most common in ちゃだめ / じゃだめ 'mustn't'. 泳ぐ has the て-form 泳いで, so では → じゃ.
JP-EX-03-007.tip: ては → ちゃ; では → じゃ.

JP-EX-03-008.notes: 見ちゃだめ 'don't look'. 見ては → 見ちゃ. It's typical of parents and friends; with a stranger, 見ないでください. Said in fun, it can tease.

JP-EX-03-009.notes: なくちゃ is the casual form of なくては (いけない): やらなくちゃ 'I've got to'. The rest of the sentence is dropped. やる = do (casual).
JP-EX-03-009.tip: なくちゃ and なきゃ = must (casual).

JP-EX-03-010.notes: なきゃ is the casual form of なければ (ならない): 行かなきゃ. It's slightly more common than なくちゃ among younger speakers.

JP-EX-03-011.notes: わかんない is a casual contraction of わからない: ら becomes ん before な. It's very casual and common among friends.
JP-EX-03-011.tip: ら / る / れ before な or の often become ん.

JP-EX-03-012.notes: つまんない is casual for つまらない (boring). The same ん contraction gives すんの (するの) and いらんない (いられない). 映画 = film.

JP-EX-03-013.notes: じゃん at the end means 'isn't it, you know': いいじゃん 'that's great'. It spread from Yokohama and the Kanto region and is now nationwide.
JP-EX-03-013.tip: じゃん = casual じゃないか.

JP-EX-03-014.notes: だから言ったじゃん 'I told you so'. じゃん here asserts something the listener should have known. The past 言った is the speaker's earlier warning. The tone is smug or exasperated.

JP-EX-03-015.notes: っけ means 'was it?', when trying to remember: 何時だったっけ. It's usually with the past form, even about the future.
JP-EX-03-015.tip: っけ = what was it again? Polite: でしたっけ.

JP-EX-03-016.notes: 名前なんだっけ 'what was the name?'. なん is 何 before だ. The polite version is お名前は何でしたっけ. あの人 = that person (both know).

JP-EX-03-017.notes: んだって means 'I heard, apparently': 結婚するんだって. It's casual hearsay, equal to そうだ. The source is unnamed; it might be gossip. Compare 結婚するらしい (apparently, slightly more distant).
JP-EX-03-017.tip: んだって = casual そうだ (I heard).

JP-EX-03-018.notes: 閉まるんだって 'apparently it's closing'. Rising intonation turns it into a question: 'is it really?'. 来月 = next month.

JP-EX-03-019.notes: っす is a clipped です used by young men to seniors in sport clubs and part-time jobs: そうっすね. In a job interview or with customers it would be too casual.
JP-EX-03-019.tip: っす = clipped です (young men to seniors).

JP-EX-03-020.notes: いいっす 'that's fine'. っす keeps a hint of politeness while sounding relaxed. Some find it sloppy. The よ adds friendliness.

JP-EX-03-021.notes: の at the end with rising intonation makes a soft casual question: 行くの? 'are you going?'. Plain 行く? is blunter.
JP-EX-03-021.tip: Casual question: plain + の? (noun + なの?).

JP-EX-03-022.notes: Nouns and な-adjectives take な before の: 本当なの? 'is it true?'. ×本当の? is wrong. The question is soft and curious rather than sceptical. A sharper version would be 本当?

JP-EX-04-001.notes: かな means 'I wonder', thinking aloud: 晴れるかな. It's neutral between men and women and very common in casual speech.
JP-EX-04-001.tip: かな = I wonder; かしら = the same, feminine and dated.

JP-EX-04-002.notes: かしら means 'I wonder' too, but sounds feminine and rather old-fashioned. It's heard from older women and in fiction.

JP-EX-04-003.notes: ぞ adds a strong assertion or warning: 危ないぞ! 'look out!'. It sounds masculine and rough. 危ない = dangerous. Women would more often say 危ない! alone or 危ないよ.

JP-EX-04-004.notes: ぜ adds a casual 'come on': 行こうぜ 'let's go'. It's masculine and a little dated, typical of manga. Women would say 行こう or 行こうよ.

JP-EX-04-005.notes: よね checks something you believe: 止まりますよね 'it stops there, right?'. It's softer than plain ね and very common when confirming facts.
JP-EX-04-005.tip: よね = checking your own belief.
JP-EX-04-005.text: この電車、渋谷に止まります{{c1::よね::right? (checking)}}。
JP-EX-04-005.tr: This train stops at Shibuya, doesn't it?
JP-EX-04-005.flag: dup: replaced 明日は休みですよね (near-identical to N5-08-018)

JP-EX-04-006.notes: だよね after a noun: 田中さんのだよね 'it's Tanaka's, isn't it?'. In casual speech だ is needed before よね after nouns.

JP-EX-04-007.notes: もん gives a childish or sulky excuse: 眠いもん 'because I'm sleepy!'. だって (but) often comes before it. 眠い = sleepy.

JP-EX-04-008.notes: んだもん 'well, I didn't know!'. Adults use it jokingly or when sulking. It's casual for ものだから. The past form plus んだ.

JP-EX-04-009.notes: な at the end is a masculine or self-directed ね: いい天気だな. It sounds relaxed and is common among men. Women would use ね.
JP-EX-04-009.tip: な = masculine or self-directed ね.

JP-EX-04-010.notes: な said to yourself: 疲れたな 'I'm tired'. Anyone can use it when talking to themselves. The speaker is reflecting, not addressing anyone. It's like a sigh.

JP-EX-04-011.notes: わ in Tokyo is a feminine softener: すてきだわ. It's now mostly heard from older women and in fiction. まあ (oh) adds to the old-fashioned feminine tone.
JP-EX-04-011.tip: わ: feminine in Tokyo; neutral in Kansai.

JP-EX-04-012.notes: わ in Kansai is a neutral assertion used by men and women alike: 帰るわ 'I'm off'. The same sound means different things by region.

JP-EX-04-013.notes: さ is a casual filler or emphasis: だからさ 'so, like'. Overusing it sounds childish. もう一回 = once more. The さ is placed mid-sentence, after だから, as a pause.

JP-EX-04-014.notes: さ attaches directly to nouns and な-adjectives, dropping だ: 大丈夫さ 'it'll be fine', not ×大丈夫ださ. At the end of a sentence it reassures casually, a bit like 'no worries'.
JP-EX-04-014.text: (To a friend) 大丈夫{{c1::さ::reassuring emphasis}}。
JP-EX-04-014.flag: text: removed だ: sentence-final さ follows a noun or な-adjective directly (大丈夫さ, not 大丈夫ださ)

JP-EX-05-001.notes: でございます is the very polite です used by shop staff: 二階でございます. 二階 is the first floor in British terms, since Japan counts the ground floor as 一階.
JP-EX-05-001.tip: 二階 = first floor (UK); 一階 = ground floor.
JP-EX-05-001.tr: The toilets are on the first floor.
JP-EX-05-001.flag: tr: 二階 is the British first floor (Japan counts the ground floor as 一階); was 'second floor'

JP-EX-05-002.notes: ございます is the very polite ある: メニューがございます. It's the standard in shops, hotels and restaurants. こちら = here (polite).

JP-EX-05-003.notes: 伺う is the humble form of 行く (and 聞く): 御社に伺います. 御社 means 'your company' in speech; in writing it's 貴社.
JP-EX-05-003.tip: 御社 (spoken) / 貴社 (written) = your company.

JP-EX-05-004.notes: 拝見する is the humble form of 見る: 資料を拝見しました. 資料 = documents, materials. 拝見 contains 拝 (worship, bow), showing deference. It's used for looking at something belonging to a superior or client.

JP-EX-05-005.notes: 存じる is the humble form of 知る: 存じております 'I'm aware'. The negative is 存じません. その件 = that matter. ている becomes ております in humble speech. It's standard in business emails.

JP-EX-05-006.notes: 申し上げる is the humble form of 言う when addressing a superior: 社長に申し上げます. It's stronger than 申す. 社長 = company president.

JP-EX-05-007.notes: ていらっしゃる is the honorific ている: 話していらっしゃいます. ておられる is a slightly weaker alternative. 電話で話す = talk on the phone. The subject is a superior, so the progressive is raised.
JP-EX-05-007.tip: Honorific ている: ていらっしゃる.

JP-EX-05-008.notes: 住んでいらっしゃいます 'lives (honorific)'. The state continues, so ている is needed. 東京に住む = live in Tokyo. The state of residing continues. The plain version would be 住んでいます.

JP-EX-05-009.notes: お + stem + ください is the honorific request: お待ちください 'please wait'. 少々 is a formal 'a little'. It's the standard phrase on the phone.
JP-EX-05-009.tip: お + stem + ください = honorific please.

JP-EX-05-010.notes: ご + noun + ください: ご記入ください 'please fill this in'. Sino-Japanese nouns usually take ご (ご記入, ご連絡) and native words お (お待ち), with exceptions such as お電話.

JP-EX-05-011.notes: ご利用いただき 'thank you for using (our service)'. ご〜いただく is humble 'receive the favour of your using'. It's on every train and bus.

JP-EX-05-012.notes: When speaking to outsiders, your own colleagues and boss count as 'inside': no さん, and humble verbs (外しております). This uchi–soto rule surprises many learners.
JP-EX-05-012.tip: To outsiders: your boss = 田中, with humble verbs.

JP-EX-05-013.notes: おっしゃる is already honorific; adding られる (おっしゃられる) makes a double honorific, common in speech but considered incorrect.
JP-EX-05-013.tip: Avoid double honorifics: おっしゃる, not ×おっしゃられる.

JP-EX-05-014.notes: ご覧になる is already honorific; ご覧になられる piles on a second honorific (られる) and is considered incorrect, though it's often heard.
JP-EX-05-014.text: 部長はもう資料を{{c1::ご覧になりました::ご覧になりました or ご覧になられました?}}。
JP-EX-05-014.tr: The manager has already looked at the documents.
JP-EX-05-014.flag: dup: replaced 部長はもうお帰りになりました (near-identical to N4-11-006); answer お帰りになりました → ご覧になりました

JP-EX-06-001.notes: である is the essay-style copula: 島国である. Reports and academic writing use である instead of です or だ. 島国 = island nation.
JP-EX-06-001.tip: Essay copula: である / ではない / であった.

JP-EX-06-002.notes: ではない is the essay-style negative copula. じゃない would be too casual in writing. 簡単な問題 = a simple problem. Essays avoid じゃない entirely.

JP-EX-06-003.notes: であった is the essay-style past copula: 重要であった. な-adjectives take である directly. 結果 = result. 重要 = important. The tone is objective and suits scientific papers.

JP-EX-06-004.notes: A verb stem can link clauses in writing: 歩き、電車に乗った. It's more formal than the て-form 歩いて. 電車に乗る = get on a train.
JP-EX-06-004.tip: Written linking: stem (歩き), く (広く), ず (言わず).

JP-EX-06-005.notes: ず links clauses in writing: 言わず 'without saying'. It's the written ないで. 部屋を出る = leave the room. The speaker narrates in written style. する becomes せず.

JP-EX-06-006.notes: い-adjectives link with く in writing: 広く、明るい. Speech uses 広くて. The two qualities are listed side by side. 広い = spacious; 明るい = bright. It's typical of property descriptions.

JP-EX-06-007.notes: のである is the essay-style のです: 問題はここにあるのである. It stresses a conclusion. 問題 = the problem. ここにある = lies here. The tone is that of an argument reaching its point.

JP-EX-06-008.notes: とされている means 'is said, is held': 効果があるとされている. It's impersonal and typical of reports. 効果 = effect, efficacy.
JP-EX-06-008.tip: とされている = is held to be.

JP-EX-06-009.notes: と考えられる means 'is thought': 上昇だと考えられる. The speaker avoids personal responsibility for the claim. 原因 = cause.

JP-EX-06-010.notes: であり links two descriptions in writing: 医者であり、作家でもある. Speech would say 医者で. The second description takes でもある: 'is also'. It's a compact written way to give two roles.

JP-EX-07-001.notes: ぬ is the classical negative, equal to ない: 見知らぬ人 'a stranger' (a person one doesn't know). It survives before nouns and in set phrases.
JP-EX-07-001.tip: ぬ = classical ない (見知らぬ, 知らぬ).

JP-EX-07-002.notes: 知らぬが仏 'not knowing is Buddha', i.e. ignorance is bliss. The proverb keeps ぬ where modern Japanese would say 知らない.

JP-EX-07-003.notes: 思わず means 'without meaning to': 思わず笑った 'couldn't help laughing'. ず is the classical negative, frozen in everyday words.
JP-EX-07-003.tip: 思わず, 相変わらず, 少なからず: fixed ず forms.

JP-EX-07-004.notes: 相変わらず means 'as ever': 相変わらず元気 'as energetic as ever'. Literally 'not changing (from before)'. 相変わらず can also be ironic.

JP-EX-07-005.notes: ざる is the classical negative before a noun: 知られざる名作 'an unknown masterpiece'. It's common in book and TV titles.

JP-EX-07-006.notes: べし is the classical 'must': 勉強すべし. する takes す before べし. It's found in maxims and old rules. The tone is lofty.

JP-EX-07-007.notes: ごとし is the classical 'is like': 過ぎたるは猶及ばざるが如し, a saying from the Analects of Confucius. Modern Japanese would use ようだ.

JP-EX-07-008.notes: 堂々と is an adverb from a たる-adjective: 堂々と述べる 'state confidently'. These Chinese-origin words take と as adverbs.
JP-EX-07-008.tip: たる-adjectives: 堂々たる + noun; 堂々と + verb.

JP-EX-07-009.notes: 堂々たる before a noun: 堂々たる演技 'a commanding performance'. たる is the classical attributive form. 演技 = performance.

JP-EX-07-010.notes: なかれ means 'do not' in literary commands: 恐れるなかれ 'fear not'. It's used in mottos and slogans. 失敗 = failure.
JP-EX-07-010.tip: Dictionary form + なかれ = do not (literary).

JP-EX-07-011.notes: かりし is the classical past of an い-adjective before a noun: 若かりし頃 'in my younger days'. It's nostalgic and literary.

JP-EX-08-001.notes: へん is the Kansai negative: 行かへん = 行かない. In Kyoto, 行かはらへん adds respect. ん (行かん) is also common. The tone is relaxed.
JP-EX-08-001.tip: Kansai: ない → へん (行かへん, 食べへん).

JP-EX-08-002.notes: 知らへん 'don't know'. そんなん is Kansai for そんなの. The same へん works with any verb. The tone is dismissive. The standard version is そんなの知らない.

JP-EX-08-003.notes: や is the Kansai copula: ほんまや = 本当だ. ほんま is Kansai for 本当. それ = that. The copula や is the hallmark of Kansai speech, heard in Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe.

JP-EX-08-004.notes: やで = だよ in Kansai: 雨やで 'it's rain, you know'. Other forms: やな (だね), やろ (だろう). 明日 = tomorrow. The で adds 'you know', like standard よ.

JP-EX-08-005.notes: ねん is the Kansai explanatory: 帰るねん = 帰るんだ. It explains or asserts gently. 今から = from now. The past form uses てん: 帰ってん (I went home).

JP-EX-08-006.notes: やねん after nouns and な-adjectives: 好きやねん = 好きなんだ. めっちゃ (really) is Kansai slang now used nationwide. The emotion is strong.

JP-EX-08-007.notes: はる is the Kansai light honorific: 帰らはった 'has gone home'. It shows friendly respect, softer than standard keigo.

JP-EX-08-008.notes: 言わはった 'said (with respect)'. Kyoto speakers use はる very widely, even for strangers. 何て = what. The polite standard is おっしゃった.

JP-EX-08-009.notes: あかん means 'no good, mustn't' = だめ: したらあかん. It's one of the best-known Kansai words. したら = if you do. The word comes from 埒が明かない (get nowhere).
JP-EX-08-009.tip: あかん = だめ; なあかん = must.

JP-EX-08-010.notes: なあかん means 'must': 行かなあかん = 行かなければならない. It's the Kansai なきゃ. もう = already, now. The ending is shortened from なければあかん. It's heard constantly in Osaka.

JP-EX-08-011.notes: やから = だから in Kansai: 雨やから. おる (be) is the Kansai いる; in standard Japanese, おる is humble. わ adds Kansai assertion.
